notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Energy is the capacity to do work.
  • Energy is a scalar quantity.
  • The SI unit of energy is joule.
  • Energy exists in many forms.
  • Major forms include mechanical, thermal, chemical, electrical, light, sound and nuclear energy.
  • Energy can be transferred from one body to another.
  • Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
  • Energy cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system.
  • The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
  • This principle is called the Law of Conservation of Energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Energy → Capacity to do Work → Joule

2. Joule
  • Joule is the SI unit of energy and work.
  • The symbol for joule is J.
  • One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of force.
  • 1 J = 1 N m.
  • 1 J = 1 kg m²/s².
  • The joule is named after James Prescott Joule.
📌 Remember

1 J = 1 N m

3. Law of Conservation of Energy
  • Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
  • Energy can only be converted from one form to another.
  • Total energy remains constant in an isolated system.
  • Mechanical energy may transform into heat because of friction.
  • Chemical energy can transform into electrical energy in a cell.
  • Electrical energy can transform into light, heat or mechanical energy.
  • Nuclear energy can transform into heat and electrical energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Conservation of Energy → Transformation, not destruction

4. Mechanical Energy
  • Mechanical energy is energy associated with motion and position.
  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy.
  • Mechanical Energy = KE + PE.
  • In an ideal frictionless system, total mechanical energy remains constant.
  • Friction can convert mechanical energy into thermal energy.
  • Loss of mechanical energy does not violate conservation of total energy.
5. Kinetic Energy
  • Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body because of its motion.
  • Kinetic energy is represented by KE.
  • KE = ½mv².
  • m is mass.
  • v is speed.
  • Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity.
  • A stationary body has zero kinetic energy.
  • Kinetic energy cannot be negative in ordinary classical mechanics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kinetic Energy → Motion → ½mv²

6. Effect of Mass on Kinetic Energy
  • Kinetic energy is directly proportional to mass when speed is constant.
  • Doubling mass doubles kinetic energy at the same speed.
  • Tripling mass triples kinetic energy at the same speed.
7. Effect of Speed on Kinetic Energy
  • Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed.
  • Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times greater.
  • Tripling speed makes kinetic energy nine times greater.
  • Halving speed reduces kinetic energy to one-fourth.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Speed × 2 → KE × 4

Speed × 3 → KE × 9

8. Potential Energy
  • Potential energy is energy associated with position or configuration.
  • Gravitational potential energy depends on height in a gravitational field.
  • Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed elastic objects.
  • Chemical energy can also be viewed as microscopic potential energy associated with molecular arrangements.
9. Gravitational Potential Energy
  • Near Earth's surface, gravitational potential energy is PE = mgh.
  • m is mass.
  • g is acceleration due to gravity.
  • h is vertical height relative to a chosen reference level.
  • SI unit is joule.
  • Greater mass gives greater gravitational potential energy at the same height.
  • Greater height gives greater gravitational potential energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gravitational PE → mgh

10. Reference Level of Potential Energy
  • Gravitational potential energy depends on the chosen reference level.
  • The zero level of potential energy can be chosen conveniently.
  • Differences in potential energy are physically important.
  • Increasing height increases gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface.
11. Elastic Potential Energy
  • Elastic potential energy is stored when an elastic body is stretched or compressed.
  • A stretched spring stores elastic potential energy.
  • A compressed spring also stores elastic potential energy.
  • For an ideal spring, elastic potential energy = ½kx².
  • k is spring constant.
  • x is extension or compression from equilibrium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spring Energy → ½kx²

12. Work
  • Work is done when a force causes displacement.
  • Work = Force × displacement in the direction of force.
  • W = Fs cosθ.
  • Work is a scalar quantity.
  • SI unit is joule.
  • Work may be positive, negative or zero.
13. Positive Work
  • Positive work occurs when force has a component in the direction of displacement.
  • Gravity does positive work on a freely falling body.
  • A person pushing a box forward does positive work if the box moves forward.
14. Negative Work
  • Negative work occurs when force acts opposite to displacement.
  • Friction commonly does negative work on a moving object.
  • Braking force does negative work on a vehicle.
  • Negative work reduces kinetic energy when it is the net work.
15. Zero Work
  • Work is zero when displacement is zero.
  • Work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement.
  • Centripetal force does zero work in ideal uniform circular motion.
  • A person holding a stationary object does zero mechanical work on the object despite biological energy expenditure.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Force present ≠ Work necessarily done

16. Work-Energy Theorem
  • The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
  • Wnet = ΔKE.
  • Positive net work increases kinetic energy.
  • Negative net work decreases kinetic energy.
  • Zero net work means kinetic energy remains unchanged.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Net Work → Change in Kinetic Energy

17. Power
  • Power is the rate of doing work.
  • Power is also the rate of energy transfer.
  • P = W/t.
  • SI unit of power is watt.
  • One watt equals one joule per second.
  • Power is a scalar quantity.
  • A more powerful machine can transfer the same energy in less time.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Power → Work/Time → Watt

18. Watt
  • Watt is the SI unit of power.
  • Symbol is W.
  • 1 W = 1 J/s.
  • The unit is named after James Watt.
  • Kilowatt is a larger unit of power.
  • 1 kW = 1000 W.
  • Megawatt is 10⁶ W.
  • Gigawatt is 10⁹ W.
19. Horsepower
  • Horsepower is a non-SI unit of power.
  • One mechanical horsepower is approximately 746 watts.
  • James Watt popularised horsepower as a way of comparing engine power.
  • Horsepower is commonly used for engines and motors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 hp ≈ 746 W

20. Electrical Energy
  • Electrical energy is associated with electric charges and electric currents.
  • Electrical energy can be converted into heat, light, sound and mechanical energy.
  • Electric motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  • Electric heaters convert electrical energy mainly into heat.
  • Electric lamps convert electrical energy into light and heat.
21. Electrical Energy Formula
  • Electrical energy consumed is E = Pt.
  • Since P = VI, electrical energy E = VIt.
  • For a resistor, E can also be written as I²Rt.
  • It can also be written as V²t/R.
  • Electrical energy in SI units is measured in joules.
22. Commercial Unit of Electrical Energy
  • The commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour.
  • Kilowatt-hour is abbreviated as kWh.
  • One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device operating for one hour.
  • 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • One kWh is commonly called one unit of electricity in household billing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Unit of Electricity → 1 kWh → 3.6 × 10⁶ J

23. Electrical Power
  • Electrical power P = VI.
  • Using Ohm's Law, P = I²R.
  • It can also be written as P = V²/R.
  • SI unit is watt.
  • Electrical appliances are rated in watts or kilowatts.
📌 Must-Memorise

P = VI

P = I²R

P = V²/R

24. Joule's Heating Effect
  • Current flowing through a resistor produces heat.
  • Heat produced H = I²Rt.
  • Heating is proportional to the square of current.
  • Heating is directly proportional to resistance and time.
  • Electric irons use the heating effect.
  • Electric heaters use the heating effect.
  • Toasters and kettles use the heating effect.
  • Fuse wires also operate through the heating effect.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joule Heating → I²Rt

25. Chemical Energy
  • Chemical energy is stored in chemical bonds and molecular arrangements.
  • Food contains chemical energy.
  • Fuels contain chemical energy.
  • Batteries and cells store chemical energy.
  • Chemical reactions can release or absorb energy.
  • Combustion converts chemical energy mainly into heat and light.
26. Energy in Food
  • Food provides chemical energy to living organisms.
  • Cellular respiration releases usable energy from nutrients.
  • ATP is the immediate energy currency of cells.
  • ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate.
  • Carbohydrates, fats and proteins can provide metabolic energy.
  • Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate or protein.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ATP → Immediate Energy Currency of Cell

27. Calorie
  • Calorie is a non-SI unit of energy.
  • One small calorie is approximately 4.184 joules.
  • A food Calorie with capital C is one kilocalorie.
  • 1 kilocalorie = 1000 calories.
  • 1 kcal ≈ 4184 J.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Food Calorie → Kilocalorie

28. Heat Energy
  • Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
  • Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body.
  • Heat is not the same as temperature.
  • SI unit of heat is joule.
  • Calorie is another commonly used heat-energy unit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Heat → Energy transfer

Temperature → Degree of hotness / thermal state

29. Temperature
  • Temperature indicates the thermal state of a body.
  • Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous heat flow.
  • Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
  • SI unit of thermodynamic temperature is kelvin.
  • Celsius is widely used in everyday measurements.
30. Internal Energy
  • Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of particles in a system.
  • Heating can increase internal energy.
  • Work done on a system can change internal energy.
  • Internal energy depends on the thermodynamic state of the system.
31. First Law of Thermodynamics
  • The First Law is an expression of conservation of energy.
  • Heat supplied to a system can increase its internal energy and/or be used to do work.
  • A common form is ΔU = Q − W when W is work done by the system.
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the first kind would violate the First Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Law → Conservation of Energy

32. Heat Transfer
  • Heat is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation.
  • Conduction mainly occurs through particle interactions without bulk movement.
  • Convection occurs through bulk movement of fluids.
  • Radiation occurs through electromagnetic waves.
  • Radiation does not require a material medium.
📌 Must-Memorise

Conduction → Mainly solids

Convection → Fluids

Radiation → No medium required

33. Conduction
  • Conduction transfers thermal energy through direct molecular or particle interactions.
  • Metals are generally good thermal conductors.
  • Wood and plastic are poor heat conductors.
  • Copper and aluminium are widely used in cookware because of good thermal conductivity.
  • Conduction does not require bulk movement of matter.
34. Convection
  • Convection occurs in liquids and gases.
  • Hot fluid generally becomes less dense and rises.
  • Cooler fluid generally descends.
  • This circulation forms convection currents.
  • Sea breeze and land breeze involve convection.
  • Boiling water exhibits convection.
35. Radiation
  • Thermal radiation consists of electromagnetic waves.
  • Radiation can travel through vacuum.
  • Heat from the Sun reaches Earth mainly by radiation.
  • All bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
  • Dark dull surfaces generally absorb and emit thermal radiation better than shiny polished surfaces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sun → Earth Heat Transfer → Radiation

36. Solar Energy
  • Solar energy originates from nuclear fusion in the Sun.
  • Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium in the Sun.
  • Part of the mass is converted into energy.
  • Solar energy reaches Earth mainly as electromagnetic radiation.
  • Solar energy drives photosynthesis.
  • Solar energy drives much of Earth's weather and climate.
  • Solar energy is renewable on human timescales.
37. Photosynthesis and Energy
  • Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
  • Green plants use sunlight to produce organic compounds.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
  • Carbon dioxide and water are used to produce glucose and oxygen in simplified representation.
  • Solar energy stored in plants enters food chains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sun → Photosynthesis → Chemical Energy → Food Chain

38. Biomass Energy
  • Biomass is organic material derived from plants and animals.
  • Biomass stores chemical energy originally derived largely from sunlight.
  • Wood, crop residues and animal waste can be used as biomass fuels.
  • Biomass is renewable when replenished sustainably.
  • Burning biomass releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants.
39. Biogas
  • Biogas is produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter.
  • Methane is the major combustible component of biogas.
  • Carbon dioxide is another major component.
  • Biogas can be produced from cattle dung, sewage and organic waste.
  • Anaerobic bacteria act in the absence of oxygen.
  • The residue from biogas plants can be used as manure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biogas → Methane → Anaerobic Digestion

40. Fossil Fuels
  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels.
  • Fossil fuels formed from ancient organic matter over geological time.
  • Fossil fuels are non-renewable on human timescales.
  • They store chemical energy.
  • Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.
  • Fossil-fuel combustion contributes to air pollution and climate change.
41. Coal
  • Coal is a solid fossil fuel.
  • It formed mainly from ancient plant material.
  • Major ranks include peat, lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite in increasing carbonisation generally.
  • Anthracite has high carbon content among major coal ranks.
  • Coal is used in thermal power generation and industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anthracite → Highest-grade common coal

42. Petroleum
  • Petroleum is a liquid fossil fuel mixture.
  • It is also called crude oil.
  • Petroleum is refined into products such as petrol, diesel, kerosene and LPG components.
  • Petroleum is an important source of transport fuels and petrochemicals.
  • It is non-renewable.
43. Natural Gas
  • Natural gas is a fossil fuel.
  • Methane is its major component.
  • Natural gas is used for electricity generation, heating and industry.
  • CNG stands for Compressed Natural Gas.
  • LNG stands for Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • Natural gas generally produces less carbon dioxide per unit energy than coal when completely combusted, though methane leakage is an important climate concern.
44. Renewable Energy
  • Renewable energy comes from sources naturally replenished on human timescales.
  • Solar energy is renewable.
  • Wind energy is renewable.
  • Hydropower is renewable.
  • Tidal energy is renewable.
  • Wave energy is renewable.
  • Geothermal energy is renewable.
  • Biomass can be renewable when sustainably managed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Renewable → Naturally Replenished

45. Non-Renewable Energy
  • Non-renewable resources are depleted much faster than they are naturally replenished.
  • Coal is non-renewable.
  • Petroleum is non-renewable.
  • Natural gas is non-renewable.
  • Uranium is a finite mineral resource and is therefore generally classified as non-renewable.
46. Solar Photovoltaic Energy
  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electrical energy.
  • Solar cells use the photovoltaic effect.
  • Semiconductor materials such as silicon are widely used.
  • Solar photovoltaic systems have no fuel combustion during operation.
  • Solar output varies with sunlight availability.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solar Cell → Light directly to Electricity

47. Solar Thermal Energy
  • Solar thermal systems convert sunlight into heat.
  • Solar water heaters use solar thermal energy.
  • Concentrated solar power uses mirrors or lenses to focus sunlight.
  • Concentrated heat may be used to produce steam and generate electricity.
48. Wind Energy
  • Wind energy converts kinetic energy of moving air into mechanical and electrical energy.
  • Wind turbines drive electrical generators.
  • Wind ultimately results largely from uneven solar heating of Earth's surface and atmospheric circulation.
  • Wind energy is renewable.
  • Electricity generation varies with wind speed.
49. Hydroelectric Energy
  • Hydropower uses the gravitational potential and kinetic energy of moving water.
  • Water stored at height possesses gravitational potential energy.
  • Falling water turns turbines.
  • Turbines drive generators.
  • Hydropower is renewable when water cycles are maintained.
  • Large dams can have ecological and social impacts.
📌 Energy Chain

Water PE → Water KE → Turbine Mechanical Energy → Electrical Energy

50. Tidal Energy
  • Tides result mainly from gravitational interactions involving the Moon and Sun.
  • Tidal energy uses periodic movement of seawater.
  • Tidal energy is renewable.
  • Tidal barrages and tidal-stream turbines can generate electricity.
  • Tides are more predictable than wind or sunlight.
51. Wave Energy
  • Wave energy captures energy from ocean surface waves.
  • Ocean waves are generated largely by wind.
  • Wind itself is driven mainly by solar heating.
  • Wave energy is renewable.
  • Commercial deployment depends strongly on location and technology.
52. Geothermal Energy
  • Geothermal energy uses heat from Earth's interior.
  • It can provide electricity and direct heating.
  • Earth's internal heat comes partly from radioactive decay and residual heat from planetary formation.
  • Geothermal energy is renewable when reservoirs are managed sustainably.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Geothermal → Earth's Internal Heat

53. Nuclear Energy
  • Nuclear energy is energy associated with changes in atomic nuclei.
  • Nuclear fission splits heavy nuclei.
  • Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei.
  • Both can release very large amounts of energy.
  • Nuclear energy involves mass-energy conversion.
  • Einstein's relation E = mc² explains mass-energy equivalence.
54. Nuclear Fission
  • Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei.
  • Fission releases energy and neutrons.
  • Uranium-235 is an important fissile isotope.
  • Plutonium-239 is also fissile.
  • Neutrons released in fission can trigger further fissions.
  • This can produce a chain reaction.
  • Controlled chain reactions are used in nuclear reactors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fission → Heavy nucleus splits

55. Nuclear Fusion
  • Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei into heavier nuclei.
  • Fusion powers the Sun and other main-sequence stars.
  • Hydrogen nuclei ultimately fuse to form helium in the Sun.
  • Fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure.
  • Fusion releases large amounts of energy.
  • Controlled fusion power remains technologically challenging.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fusion → Light nuclei combine → Stars

56. Fission vs Fusion
  • Fission splits a heavy nucleus.
  • Fusion combines light nuclei.
  • Nuclear reactors presently generate commercial electricity mainly through fission.
  • The Sun produces energy mainly through fusion.
  • Both involve conversion of some mass into energy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Nuclear Reactor → Fission

Sun → Fusion

57. Chain Reaction
  • A nuclear chain reaction occurs when neutrons from one fission cause additional fissions.
  • An uncontrolled chain reaction releases energy rapidly.
  • A controlled chain reaction is maintained in a nuclear reactor.
  • Control rods absorb excess neutrons.
58. Nuclear Reactor
  • A nuclear reactor maintains a controlled fission chain reaction.
  • Fuel contains fissile material.
  • A moderator slows fast neutrons in many reactor designs.
  • Control rods absorb neutrons.
  • Coolant removes heat.
  • Heat can produce steam.
  • Steam drives turbines connected to generators.
📌 Energy Chain

Nuclear → Heat → Steam → Turbine → Electrical

59. Moderator
  • A moderator slows down fast neutrons.
  • Slow neutrons are more effective in sustaining fission of uranium-235 in thermal reactors.
  • Heavy water can be used as a moderator.
  • Graphite can also be used as a moderator.
  • Ordinary water serves as moderator in many reactor types.
60. Control Rods
  • Control rods absorb neutrons.
  • Boron and cadmium are examples of neutron-absorbing materials.
  • Inserting control rods farther into the reactor reduces the reaction rate.
  • Withdrawing them can increase the reaction rate under controlled conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Control Rod → Absorbs Neutrons

61. Heavy Water
  • Heavy water is D₂O.
  • It contains deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen.
  • Deuterium is an isotope of hydrogen.
  • Heavy water is used as moderator and coolant in some nuclear reactors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heavy Water → D₂O

62. Energy from Mass
  • Einstein's relation is E = mc².
  • c is the speed of light.
  • c is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Because c² is very large, a small mass corresponds to a large quantity of energy.
  • Nuclear reactions involve detectable mass defects.
63. Binding Energy
  • Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
  • It is related to the mass defect.
  • Mass defect is the difference between the mass of a nucleus and the sum of the masses of its separated nucleons.
  • Greater binding energy per nucleon generally indicates greater nuclear stability over much of the periodic table.
  • Iron-group nuclei lie near the maximum binding energy per nucleon.
64. Energy Efficiency
  • Efficiency measures how much input energy becomes useful output energy.
  • Efficiency = Useful output energy / Input energy × 100%.
  • Efficiency cannot exceed 100% for an ordinary energy-conversion device.
  • Some input energy is usually dissipated as heat, sound or friction.
  • Improving efficiency reduces wasted energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Efficiency = Useful Output / Input × 100%

65. Energy Dissipation
  • Dissipation means energy becomes spread into less useful forms, often thermal energy.
  • Friction dissipates mechanical energy as heat.
  • Electrical resistance converts electrical energy into heat.
  • Total energy remains conserved despite dissipation.
  • Dissipated energy is harder to convert completely back into useful work.
66. Energy Transformation — Electric Fan
  • Electrical energy enters the fan motor.
  • The motor converts electrical energy into mechanical rotational energy.
  • Some energy becomes heat and sound.
  • The useful output is mainly kinetic energy of moving air.
67. Energy Transformation — Electric Bulb
  • Electrical energy is supplied to the lamp.
  • It is converted into light and thermal energy.
  • Incandescent lamps convert a large fraction into heat.
  • LEDs convert a larger fraction of input electricity into visible light than incandescent lamps.
68. Energy Transformation — Battery
  • A discharging battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
  • A rechargeable battery converts electrical energy into stored chemical energy while charging.
  • Energy conversion in real batteries is not perfectly efficient.
69. Energy Transformation — Generator
  • A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  • It works on electromagnetic induction.
  • Turbines can provide the mechanical energy.
  • Faraday's law is fundamental to generator operation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Generator → Mechanical to Electrical

70. Energy Transformation — Motor
  • An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  • Magnetic force on current-carrying conductors produces torque.
  • Motors are used in fans, pumps and machines.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Motor → Electrical to Mechanical

71. Energy Transformation — Hydroelectric Plant
  • Water stored in a reservoir has gravitational potential energy.
  • Falling water gains kinetic energy.
  • Water rotates a turbine.
  • The turbine has mechanical energy.
  • The generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
72. Energy Transformation — Thermal Power Plant
  • Chemical energy in fuel is released as heat.
  • Heat converts water into high-pressure steam.
  • Steam turns a turbine.
  • Turbine mechanical energy drives a generator.
  • Generator produces electrical energy.
📌 Energy Chain

Chemical → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical

73. Energy Transformation — Nuclear Power Plant
  • Nuclear fission releases nuclear energy as heat.
  • Heat produces steam.
  • Steam rotates a turbine.
  • Turbine drives a generator.
  • Electrical energy is generated.
📌 Energy Chain

Nuclear → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical

74. Energy Transformation — Solar Cell
  • Solar cell converts radiant solar energy directly into electrical energy.
  • No turbine is required in photovoltaic conversion.
  • Semiconductor junctions produce voltage when illuminated.
75. Energy Transformation — Human Body
  • Chemical energy in food is released through metabolism.
  • Energy is used for muscle contraction.
  • Mechanical work can be produced.
  • Heat is also produced.
  • Some energy supports biochemical reactions and cellular maintenance.
76. Energy Transformation — Photosynthesis
  • Solar radiation provides light energy.
  • Photosynthetic organisms convert light energy into chemical energy.
  • Chemical energy is stored in organic compounds.
  • This energy becomes available to consumers through food chains.
77. Energy Transformation — Loudspeaker
  • Electrical energy is converted into mechanical vibration.
  • Mechanical vibration produces sound energy.
  • Some energy is dissipated as heat.
78. Energy Transformation — Microphone
  • Sound energy causes mechanical vibration.
  • The microphone converts mechanical vibration into an electrical signal.
  • It is effectively the reverse energy-conversion role of a loudspeaker in basic description.
79. Energy Transformation — Torch
  • Chemical energy is stored in the battery.
  • Chemical energy converts into electrical energy.
  • Electrical energy converts into light and heat.
📌 Energy Chain

Chemical → Electrical → Light + Heat

80. Energy Transformation — Car
  • Fuel contains chemical energy.
  • Combustion converts chemical energy into thermal energy.
  • Engine converts part of thermal energy into mechanical energy.
  • Mechanical energy moves the vehicle.
  • Significant energy is lost as heat and sound.
81. Potential to Kinetic Energy
  • A falling body loses gravitational potential energy.
  • Its kinetic energy increases.
  • In ideal free fall without air resistance, loss in PE equals gain in KE.
  • Total mechanical energy remains constant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PE ↓ → KE ↑

82. Pendulum Energy
  • At an extreme position, potential energy is maximum.
  • At an extreme position, kinetic energy is zero momentarily.
  • At the lowest or equilibrium position, kinetic energy is maximum.
  • At the lowest position, gravitational potential energy is minimum.
  • In an ideal pendulum, total mechanical energy remains constant.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pendulum extreme → PE max, KE zero

Centre → KE max, PE min

83. Roller-Coaster Energy
  • At the top of a hill, gravitational potential energy is high.
  • During descent, potential energy converts into kinetic energy.
  • At lower points, kinetic energy is greater.
  • Friction converts part of mechanical energy into heat and sound.
84. Energy and Momentum
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different quantities.
  • Momentum p = mv.
  • Kinetic energy KE = ½mv².
  • Momentum is a vector.
  • Kinetic energy is a scalar.
  • Momentum can be zero when vector momenta cancel while total kinetic energy remains non-zero.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Momentum conserved ≠ Kinetic energy always conserved.

85. Elastic Collision
  • Total momentum is conserved.
  • Total kinetic energy is conserved.
  • Ideal elastic collisions occur approximately in certain particle interactions.
  • Kinetic energy is transferred among colliding objects without net loss to deformation or heat in the ideal case.
86. Inelastic Collision
  • Momentum remains conserved in an isolated system.
  • Kinetic energy is not conserved as kinetic energy.
  • Some kinetic energy changes into heat, sound or deformation.
  • In a perfectly inelastic collision, objects stick together.
87. Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
  • In ideal SHM, total mechanical energy is constant.
  • At equilibrium, kinetic energy is maximum.
  • At equilibrium, potential energy is minimum.
  • At extreme positions, kinetic energy is zero.
  • At extreme positions, potential energy is maximum.
88. Energy Stored in Capacitor
  • A charged capacitor stores electrical potential energy.
  • Stored energy = ½CV².
  • C is capacitance.
  • V is potential difference.
  • Capacitors can release energy rapidly.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Capacitor Energy → ½CV²

89. Energy Stored in Inductor
  • An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.
  • Stored magnetic energy = ½LI².
  • L is inductance.
  • I is current.
90. Light Energy
  • Light is electromagnetic radiation.
  • Light carries energy and momentum.
  • Light can travel through vacuum.
  • The energy of a photon is E = hf.
  • h is Planck's constant.
  • f is frequency.
  • Higher-frequency photons have greater energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Photon Energy → E = hf

91. Planck's Constant
  • Planck's constant is represented by h.
  • Its exact SI value is 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
  • Max Planck introduced the quantum concept in explaining black-body radiation.
  • Photon energy is proportional to frequency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Max Planck → E = hf

92. Frequency and Photon Energy
  • Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency.
  • Higher frequency means greater photon energy.
  • Gamma rays have higher photon energy than visible light.
  • Radio waves have lower photon energy than visible light.
  • Within visible light, violet photons have more energy than red photons.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Violet → Higher frequency and energy

Red → Lower frequency and energy

93. Sound Energy
  • Sound is a mechanical wave.
  • Sound requires a material medium.
  • Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
  • Sound carries energy from one location to another.
  • Sound waves involve particle oscillations about equilibrium positions.
94. Energy and Frequency of Sound
  • Frequency determines pitch.
  • Greater amplitude generally corresponds to greater sound intensity.
  • Loudness is related to intensity and human perception.
  • Sound energy increases with wave amplitude.
95. Renewable vs Non-Renewable — Must Remember
  • Solar → Renewable.
  • Wind → Renewable.
  • Hydropower → Renewable.
  • Tidal → Renewable.
  • Wave → Renewable.
  • Geothermal → Renewable.
  • Biomass → Renewable if sustainably replenished.
  • Coal → Non-renewable.
  • Petroleum → Non-renewable.
  • Natural gas → Non-renewable.
  • Uranium → Non-renewable mineral resource.
96. Energy Conservation and Sustainable Use
  • Energy conservation in everyday language means reducing unnecessary energy consumption.
  • This differs from the physical Law of Conservation of Energy.
  • Efficient appliances reduce energy demand.
  • Insulation reduces unwanted heat transfer.
  • Public transport can reduce energy use per passenger under suitable conditions.
  • Renewable-energy deployment can reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Physical conservation of energy → Energy cannot be destroyed.

Energy conservation policy → Avoiding waste and using energy efficiently.

97. Energy Star Ratings
  • Energy-efficiency labels help compare electricity consumption of appliances.
  • In India, the Bureau of Energy Efficiency operates star-labelling programmes for various appliances.
  • More efficient appliances use less electricity for comparable useful output.
  • BEE stands for Bureau of Energy Efficiency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

BEE → Energy Efficiency

98. Bureau of Energy Efficiency
  • Bureau of Energy Efficiency is abbreviated as BEE.
  • BEE functions under the Ministry of Power, Government of India.
  • It was established under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.
  • BEE promotes efficient use of energy.
  • Standards and labelling are important BEE programmes.
99. Energy Conservation Act
  • India's Energy Conservation Act was enacted in 2001.
  • It provides the legal framework for promoting energy efficiency.
  • The Act led to establishment of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency.
  • Energy-efficiency standards can reduce electricity consumption.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Energy Conservation Act → 2001 → BEE

100. Energy Audit
  • An energy audit evaluates how energy is used in a building or industrial system.
  • It identifies opportunities to reduce energy waste.
  • Energy audits can improve efficiency and reduce operating costs.
  • Industrial energy management often uses energy audits.
101. Pumped-Storage Hydropower
  • Pumped storage stores energy using gravitational potential energy of water.
  • During low-demand periods, electricity pumps water to a higher reservoir.
  • During high demand, water flows downward through turbines.
  • Pumped storage is an energy-storage method rather than a primary energy source.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pumped Storage → Electrical ↔ Gravitational PE

102. Battery Energy Storage
  • Batteries store energy chemically.
  • During discharge, chemical energy converts into electrical energy.
  • During charging of rechargeable batteries, electrical energy is stored chemically.
  • Batteries help balance variable renewable power sources.
103. Hydrogen as Energy Carrier
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier rather than a primary energy source in most applications.
  • Hydrogen can be produced by electrolysis of water.
  • Electrolysis requires electrical energy.
  • Hydrogen fuel cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
  • Water is a main reaction product in hydrogen fuel cells using oxygen.
  • Climate impact depends on how hydrogen is produced.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hydrogen → Energy carrier, not automatically an energy source.

104. Fuel Cell
  • A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy through electrochemical reactions.
  • Hydrogen fuel cells combine hydrogen and oxygen electrochemically.
  • Water and heat are products in a basic hydrogen fuel cell.
  • Fuel cells are not the same as conventional combustion engines.
105. Primary Energy
  • Primary energy is energy available directly from natural sources before conversion.
  • Coal is a primary energy source.
  • Crude oil is a primary energy source.
  • Sunlight is a primary energy source.
  • Wind is a primary energy source.
  • Uranium is a primary energy resource.
106. Secondary Energy
  • Secondary energy is produced by converting primary energy.
  • Electricity is generally a secondary energy carrier.
  • Petrol is produced by refining crude oil.
  • Hydrogen produced using another energy source is a secondary energy carrier.
  • Secondary energy is easier to distribute or use in many applications.
107. Energy Density
  • Energy density indicates energy stored per unit mass or volume.
  • Fuels differ greatly in energy density.
  • Nuclear fuels have extremely high energy density compared with chemical fuels.
  • Batteries generally have lower energy density than liquid hydrocarbon fuels by mass.
108. Energy and Efficiency of Machines
  • No real machine converts all input energy into useful output energy.
  • Friction causes energy dissipation.
  • Heat and sound are common unwanted energy outputs.
  • Efficiency can be improved by reducing friction and heat loss.
  • Lubrication reduces frictional energy losses.
109. Perpetual Motion Machine
  • A perpetual-motion machine is a hypothetical machine operating indefinitely without an external energy source or producing more energy than supplied.
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the first kind violates conservation of energy.
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
  • No genuine perpetual-motion machine has been demonstrated.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Perpetual Motion → Impossible under thermodynamic laws

110. Energy and Einstein
  • Albert Einstein established mass-energy equivalence.
  • E = mc².
  • Mass can be converted into other forms of energy in nuclear processes.
  • Energy also contributes to the mass of a system.
  • The relation is central to nuclear physics.
111. James Prescott Joule
  • James Prescott Joule studied the relationship between mechanical work and heat.
  • His work helped establish conservation of energy.
  • The SI unit of energy is named joule in his honour.
  • Joule also studied electrical heating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

James Joule → Energy + Heating Effect

112. James Watt
  • James Watt made major improvements to the steam engine.
  • The SI unit of power, watt, is named after him.
  • Watt popularised the term horsepower.
  • Power and energy are different quantities.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Joule → Energy

Watt → Power

113. Max Planck
  • Max Planck introduced the quantum hypothesis.
  • He proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets in his treatment of black-body radiation.
  • Photon energy relation is E = hf.
  • The Planck constant is represented by h.
  • Planck received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918.
114. Energy Units
  • SI unit of energy → Joule.
  • Commercial electrical-energy unit → kWh.
  • Food-energy unit commonly used → kilocalorie.
  • Atomic and nuclear energies are often expressed in electronvolts.
  • 1 eV is the energy gained by one elementary charge moving through a potential difference of one volt.
  • 1 eV ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 eV ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

115. Electronvolt
  • Electronvolt is abbreviated as eV.
  • It is a unit of energy, not electric potential.
  • keV means kilo-electronvolt.
  • MeV means mega-electronvolt.
  • GeV means giga-electronvolt.
  • Electronvolt is widely used in atomic, nuclear and particle physics.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

eV → Energy

Volt → Potential difference

116. Important Energy Formulae
  • Work → W = Fs cosθ.
  • Kinetic energy → KE = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy → PE = mgh.
  • Elastic potential energy → ½kx².
  • Power → P = W/t.
  • Electrical power → P = VI.
  • Electrical energy → E = Pt = VIt.
  • Joule heating → H = I²Rt.
  • Mass-energy equivalence → E = mc².
  • Photon energy → E = hf.
  • Capacitor energy → ½CV².
  • Inductor energy → ½LI².
  • Efficiency → Useful output/Input × 100%.
117. Important Energy Units
  • Energy → Joule.
  • Work → Joule.
  • Heat → Joule.
  • Power → Watt.
  • Electrical energy billing → kWh.
  • Food energy → kcal.
  • Atomic energy → eV.
  • 1 kWh → 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • 1 calorie → 4.184 J.
  • 1 kcal → 4184 J.
  • 1 hp → About 746 W.
118. Must-Memorise Energy Transformations
  • Generator → Mechanical to electrical.
  • Motor → Electrical to mechanical.
  • Battery discharge → Chemical to electrical.
  • Battery charging → Electrical to chemical.
  • Electric heater → Electrical to heat.
  • Bulb → Electrical to light + heat.
  • Solar cell → Light to electrical.
  • Photosynthesis → Light to chemical.
  • Hydropower → Potential to kinetic to mechanical to electrical.
  • Thermal plant → Chemical to thermal to mechanical to electrical.
  • Nuclear plant → Nuclear to thermal to mechanical to electrical.
  • Loudspeaker → Electrical to sound.
  • Microphone → Sound to electrical.
  • Human body → Chemical to mechanical + heat.
119. TNPSC Traps
  • Energy is a scalar quantity.
  • Force is vector; energy is scalar.
  • Joule is the SI unit of both work and energy.
  • Watt is unit of power, not energy.
  • kWh is a unit of energy, not power.
  • One household electricity unit equals one kWh.
  • 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • Kinetic energy depends on velocity squared.
  • Momentum depends linearly on velocity.
  • Mechanical energy can decrease due to friction while total energy remains conserved.
  • Potential-energy zero level is arbitrary.
  • Power measures rate of energy transfer.
  • Heat and temperature are different.
  • Heat flows naturally from hotter to colder bodies.
  • Radiation does not require a material medium.
  • Sound requires a medium.
  • Solar energy originates from nuclear fusion.
  • Current commercial nuclear power mainly uses fission.
  • Strong heat from the Sun is produced by fusion, not combustion.
  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable.
  • Uranium is also non-renewable.
  • Solar, wind, hydropower, tidal and geothermal are renewable.
  • Biomass is renewable only if replenished sustainably.
  • Hydrogen is usually an energy carrier.
  • Electricity is usually a secondary energy carrier.
  • Energy efficiency can never exceed 100% for ordinary devices.
  • A perpetual-motion machine violates fundamental thermodynamic laws.
  • Joule is associated with energy.
  • Watt is associated with power.
  • eV is a unit of energy, not voltage.
  • Food Calorie means kilocalorie.
120. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Energy → Capacity to work.
  • Unit → Joule.
  • KE → ½mv².
  • PE → mgh.
  • Spring energy → ½kx².
  • Mechanical energy → KE + PE.
  • Work → Fs cosθ.
  • Work-energy → Wnet = ΔKE.
  • Power → W/t.
  • Watt → J/s.
  • 1 hp → 746 W.
  • Electrical power → VI.
  • 1 unit → 1 kWh.
  • 1 kWh → 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • Heat transfer → Conduction + Convection + Radiation.
  • Sun → Fusion.
  • Reactor → Fission.
  • Solar cell → Light to electricity.
  • Generator → Mechanical to electrical.
  • Motor → Electrical to mechanical.
  • Battery → Chemical ↔ Electrical.
  • ATP → Cellular energy currency.
  • Biogas → Methane.
  • Renewable → Solar, wind, hydro.
  • Fossil fuels → Non-renewable.
  • Efficiency → Useful/Input × 100.
  • Einstein → E = mc².
  • Planck → E = hf.
  • Joule → Energy.
  • Watt → Power.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Energy means? → Capacity to do work.
  • SI unit of energy? → Joule.
  • Energy is scalar or vector? → Scalar.
  • 1 joule equals? → 1 N m.
  • Scientist after whom joule is named? → James Prescott Joule.
  • Law stating energy cannot be created or destroyed? → Law of Conservation of Energy.
  • Mechanical energy equals? → Kinetic energy + Potential energy.
  • Energy due to motion? → Kinetic energy.
  • Kinetic-energy formula? → ½mv².
  • If speed doubles, KE becomes? → Four times.
  • If speed triples, KE becomes? → Nine times.
  • Energy due to position? → Potential energy.
  • Gravitational potential-energy formula? → mgh.
  • Elastic potential-energy formula? → ½kx².
  • Work formula? → Fs cosθ.
  • SI unit of work? → Joule.
  • Net work equals? → Change in kinetic energy.
  • This relation is called? → Work-Energy Theorem.
  • Rate of doing work? → Power.
  • Power formula? → W/t.
  • SI unit of power? → Watt.
  • 1 watt equals? → 1 J/s.
  • 1 horsepower approximately? → 746 W.
  • Electrical-power formula? → P = VI.
  • Other electrical power formulas? → I²R and V²/R.
  • Electrical-energy formula? → E = Pt.
  • Commercial unit of electrical energy? → Kilowatt-hour.
  • One unit of household electricity? → 1 kWh.
  • 1 kWh equals? → 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • Joule-heating formula? → I²Rt.
  • Chemical energy in cells is converted to? → Electrical energy during discharge.
  • Immediate cellular energy currency? → ATP.
  • ATP stands for? → Adenosine triphosphate.
  • Food Calorie means? → Kilocalorie.
  • 1 calorie approximately? → 4.184 J.
  • 1 kcal approximately? → 4184 J.
  • Heat means? → Energy transferred because of temperature difference.
  • SI unit of heat? → Joule.
  • SI temperature unit? → Kelvin.
  • Natural direction of heat flow? → Hotter body to colder body.
  • Three modes of heat transfer? → Conduction, convection and radiation.
  • Heat transfer mainly through solids without bulk movement? → Conduction.
  • Heat transfer through bulk fluid movement? → Convection.
  • Heat transfer possible through vacuum? → Radiation.
  • How does solar heat reach Earth? → Radiation.
  • Source of Sun's energy? → Nuclear fusion.
  • Main nuclear process in Sun? → Hydrogen fusion to helium.
  • Photosynthesis converts? → Light energy to chemical energy.
  • Major combustible gas in biogas? → Methane.
  • Biogas formation occurs mainly through? → Anaerobic decomposition.
  • Three fossil fuels? → Coal, petroleum and natural gas.
  • Are fossil fuels renewable? → No.
  • Highest-grade common coal? → Anthracite.
  • Main component of natural gas? → Methane.
  • CNG stands for? → Compressed Natural Gas.
  • LNG stands for? → Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • Examples of renewable energy? → Solar, wind, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal and sustainable biomass.
  • Is uranium renewable? → No.
  • Solar photovoltaic cell converts? → Light directly into electricity.
  • Wind turbine converts? → Wind kinetic energy into mechanical and then electrical energy.
  • Hydropower initially uses? → Gravitational potential energy of water.
  • Tidal energy mainly derives from? → Gravitational interaction of Moon and Sun with Earth.
  • Geothermal energy comes from? → Earth's internal heat.
  • Nuclear fission means? → Splitting a heavy nucleus.
  • Nuclear fusion means? → Combining light nuclei.
  • Current nuclear reactors mainly use? → Fission.
  • Sun uses? → Fusion.
  • Common fissile isotope? → Uranium-235.
  • Another fissile isotope? → Plutonium-239.
  • Purpose of moderator? → Slow neutrons.
  • Examples of moderator? → Heavy water, graphite or ordinary water depending on reactor.
  • Purpose of control rods? → Absorb excess neutrons.
  • Materials used in control rods? → Boron and cadmium.
  • Heavy water formula? → D₂O.
  • Einstein's mass-energy equation? → E = mc².
  • Speed of light approximately? → 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Mass defect is related to? → Nuclear binding energy.
  • Efficiency formula? → Useful output/Input × 100%.
  • Can ordinary machine efficiency exceed 100%? → No.
  • Generator converts? → Mechanical to electrical energy.
  • Motor converts? → Electrical to mechanical energy.
  • Solar cell converts? → Light to electrical energy.
  • Battery discharge converts? → Chemical to electrical energy.
  • Battery charging converts? → Electrical to chemical energy.
  • Thermal power plant energy sequence? → Chemical → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical.
  • Nuclear power plant energy sequence? → Nuclear → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical.
  • Hydroelectric plant sequence? → Gravitational PE → KE → Mechanical → Electrical.
  • At pendulum extreme position? → PE maximum, KE zero.
  • At pendulum mean position? → KE maximum, PE minimum.
  • Momentum is scalar or vector? → Vector.
  • Kinetic energy is scalar or vector? → Scalar.
  • Is kinetic energy conserved in every collision? → No.
  • Kinetic energy conserved in? → Elastic collision.
  • Momentum conserved in isolated inelastic collision? → Yes.
  • Capacitor stores energy in? → Electric field.
  • Capacitor-energy formula? → ½CV².
  • Inductor stores energy in? → Magnetic field.
  • Inductor-energy formula? → ½LI².
  • Photon-energy formula? → E = hf.
  • Scientist associated with quantum energy relation? → Max Planck.
  • Planck constant unit? → J s.
  • Higher photon frequency means? → Higher photon energy.
  • Which visible photon has more energy, violet or red? → Violet.
  • Does sound travel in vacuum? → No.
  • Does light travel in vacuum? → Yes.
  • Physical energy-conservation law means? → Energy cannot be created or destroyed.
  • Everyday energy conservation means? → Reducing waste and improving efficiency.
  • BEE stands for? → Bureau of Energy Efficiency.
  • BEE functions under? → Ministry of Power.
  • Energy Conservation Act enacted in? → 2001.
  • Energy audit means? → Assessment of energy use and efficiency opportunities.
  • Pumped-storage hydropower stores energy mainly as? → Gravitational potential energy.
  • Hydrogen is generally classified as? → Energy carrier.
  • Fuel cell converts? → Chemical energy directly into electrical energy.
  • Electricity is generally primary or secondary energy? → Secondary energy.
  • Electronvolt is unit of? → Energy.
  • 1 eV approximately? → 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  • Is eV a unit of voltage? → No.
  • Scientist associated with joule? → James Prescott Joule.
  • Scientist associated with watt? → James Watt.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; Power = W/t; 1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; Sun → Fusion; Reactor → Fission; Energy is conserved.
